fields.title: Lozhka: acquisition cost doubled
fields.summary: Ads cost twice as much, only a third make a second order. Decide what to do about growth.
fields.decisionPrompt: How will you grow in the next quarter?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager at Lozhka.
fields.brief/company: Lozhka is a fictional meal plan delivery service: 11 000 active clients across three cities, average check 5 400 ₽ for a week of meals.
fields.brief/context: Over six months, acquisition cost grew from 2 100 to 4 300 ₽. The investor expects 40% client growth per quarter. Marketing suggests working with influencers, Sales suggests offering a promo code for the first order.
fields.brief/objective: Decide how to grow in the next quarter.
fields.brief/constraints: Budget of 4 million for the quarter; the kitchen can handle growth up to one and a half times without adding a new shift.
fields.brief/task: Choose a direction and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: A discount buys the first order and ruins the second
fields.learnTakeaway/body: When a client pays off from the second purchase, the repeat rate is the main acquisition metric. Discounted ad creative brings people who came for the discount, and cohorts deteriorate quietly: lead cost stays the same, but pay-off disappears. Before looking for a new channel, check who the current one brings and what stops those who tried from returning.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Average check 5 400 ₽, margin after COGS and delivery is 1 900 ₽ per order.

Current CAC is 4 300 ₽. This means a client pays off on the second order, not earlier.

Share of users making a second order: 34%. Third order: 26%. Beyond that, the curve is almost flat: those who reach the third order stay for 9 weeks on average.

By cohorts over six months: the second-order rate dropped from 47% to 34%. Average check did not change.

During the same six-month period, Marketing shifted its primary channel: previously search and referrals, now 70% of the budget goes to social media feeds with '40% discount on the first week' creatives.

Among discount signups, 19% make a second order; among others, 52%.
fields.evidenceCards/1/title: What happens after the first order
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Survey of churned users (312 responses): 'too expensive' — 38%, 'menu didn't fit' — 27%, 'inconvenient delivery time' — 19%, 'just trying out' — 16%.

Support: main first-week inquiry is 'can I swap a meal in the plan'. Currently impossible: meal plans are fixed.

The app has no way to give meal feedback: ratings go to delivery, not the food.

Those who used delivery rescheduling at least once (available, but hidden on the third screen) make a second order in 58% of cases.

Repeat orders are placed from scratch: the previous meal plan is not saved and cannot be repeated with one tap.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Social feed: 70% of budget, CAC 4 300 ₽, high capacity, but cost has been rising for three quarters in a row.

Search 'healthy meal delivery + city': 12% of budget, CAC 2 600 ₽, but volume is limited — almost all available traffic is bought out.

Referrals: 14% of clients come via recommendation, CAC close to zero, second order rate 61%. No referral program — people share on their own.

Influencers: not tried. Agency estimate — 700k ₽ for 4 placements, predicted CAC 3 000 ₽ 'based on other clients' experience'.

Kitchen: current shift handles 16 000 orders per week, currently at 11 000.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Three notable competitors: a premium service with custom meal plans (twice as expensive), and two mass-market services at roughly the same price.

On Lozhka's website: 'Healthy food delivery. Tasty, healthy, convenient.'

In 20 interviews with clients ordering for over two months, one theme recurs: 'I stopped worrying about what to cook on Wednesday evening.' Only two mentioned calories or health.

All three competitors talk about health and calories in their ads.

Among regular clients, 64% are families with children where one person cooks. Ad creatives show people at the gym.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Fix second orders and restore economics
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Find out why second orders dropped from 47% to 34%, eliminate the cause, and reallocate the budget back to channels that bring retained users.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
Breakdown by source gives an answer in half a day: those coming via discount place a second order in 19% of cases versus 52% for the rest. The drop from 47% to 34% is a change in channel and creative, not product degradation.
You remove the 40% discount from main creative, keeping it in one segment to test. You shift part of the budget to search, buying out all available volume.
In the product, you do three things: reorder previous plan with one button, move delivery to the first screen (users who used it have a 58% second order rate), and allow replacing two dishes in the plan.
You launch a referral program: 14% come via recommendation on their own, CAC near zero, second order at 61%.
Over the quarter, clients are +38%—slightly below target—but CAC is 3 100 ₽ and payback comes from the second order. The kitchen handles it.
Trade-off: the client count target was not met exactly, and the conversation with the investor had to be backed by payback numbers.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Growth target is 40%, current channel is getting expensive. Agency promises 3 000 ₽ CAC — cheaper than current. Buy four placements for 700k.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Two out of four placements bring a noticeable surge in orders, two bring almost nothing. Average CAC ends up at 3 900 ₽ instead of promised 3 000 ₽.
Second order rate for influencer traffic is 24%: audience tries by recommendation, not out of need.
Cannot be repeated: prices for a second run are raised, and the surge is not reproducible.
The kitchen fails in the week following placement: 300 orders are delayed, and some of those clients never return.
Trade-off: picked a channel based on someone else's estimate without a small test or threshold, leaving the main leak — 34% second order rate — unaddressed.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Offer a promo code for the first order
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: In the survey, 38% say 'too expensive'. A promo code lowers friction and will bring volume quickly.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
First orders indeed grow by 44% — growth target looks achievable.
However, second orders drop further: to 17% for the promo cohort. Exactly what happened over the past six months with the 40% discount, only worse.
First-order margin drops to zero, pushing pay-off to the third order, which very few reach.
After a quarter, active clients are up 9%, but cash for the next quarter is depleted.
Trade-off: amplified the exact root cause that degraded cohorts, acting on the word 'expensive', even though data shows second orders dropped for discount signups, not full-price buyers.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: We say what everyone says: 'tasty, healthy, convenient'. Take 'stopped worrying about what to cook on Wednesday evening' from interviews, switch creatives and target families.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
Correct observation and strong messaging: competitors talk calories, loyal clients talk about offloading mental load, and 64% are families, not gym-goers.
Changing creatives reduces CAC from 4 300 to 3 600 ₽ over the quarter — a solid result for little money.
However, second order rate remains at 34%: repeating a meal plan is still impossible, swapping meals is impossible, delivery rescheduling stays hidden.
By end of quarter, clients +21%, unit economics slightly better, target missed.
Trade-off: addressed only half the problem — acquisition got cheaper, but retention (which drives payback) was left untouched.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Channel chosen by popularity rather than intent and testable bet
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Acquisition cost evaluated by leads, without conversion to payment or payback
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Bottleneck identified by lowest percentage rather than highest leverage
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Failed to find the action after which churn stops
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: Retention mechanic does not match the natural frequency of the task
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: Differentiation defined as 'better at everything', which means nothing
